Class FastClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm

java.lang.Object
sootup.callgraph.AbstractCallGraphAlgorithm
sootup.callgraph.ClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm
sootup.callgraph.FastClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm
All Implemented Interfaces:
CallGraphAlgorithm
public class FastClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm extends ClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm
A variant of ClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm that resolves a virtual or interface call over the subtypes of the static type of the receiver local, instead of the subtypes of the class the invoked method reference names. This is how Soot's CHA resolves calls.

How it differs from CHA

For A a = new B(); a.m(); the bytecode refers to A.m(), but the Jimple local holding the receiver is typed B, the type inferred from the assignments to it. CHA resolves the call to A.m() and every override of m() in the subtypes of A. This algorithm resolves it to the method that B and each subtype of B declares or inherits - every subtype, whether the program instantiates it or not. When the local's type is the referenced class itself, or not a subtype of it, both algorithms agree.

The difference matters most for the methods of java.lang.Object: dx and d8 encode toString() on a local of an interface type as a call to java.lang.Object, which CHA resolves to every toString() of the program. In Android apps that bundle large libraries, e.g. Kotlin coroutines, this alone can make a call graph orders of magnitude larger.

Caveats

  • The result depends on how the bodies were typed. The referenced class comes from the bytecode, and the JVM's verifier checks the receiver against it; the type of a local is inferred by the body interceptors. Without a LocalSplitter before typing, a local that holds a B and later a C is typed with their common supertype, so the same program gives a larger call graph. A LocalPacker that merges locals of different types widens them the same way.
  • It relies on the type of each local being a supertype of every value assigned to it. The TypeAssigner guarantees this for bytecode. Bodies typed another way, e.g. Jimple files or bodies built or changed in code, must keep it; otherwise calls on a wrongly typed local silently lose edges.
  • Locals without a class type, e.g. untyped locals of dex bodies before a TypeAssigner ran, are resolved like CHA does.
  • It is not class hierarchy analysis in the textbook sense, which uses the declared type of the source: the inferred type of a local carries information about the allocations assigned to it.

How to use it

Create the view's bodies with interceptors that split the locals and then assign their types, in this order, e.g. LocalSplitter followed by TypeAssigner, and don't merge locals of different types afterwards. This is what Soot's jb pack does for every body, which is why Soot's CHA can rely on the types of locals.

    • resolveCall

      protected @NonNull Stream<MethodSignature> resolveCall(SootMethod method, InvokableStmt invokableStmt)
      Description copied from class: ClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm
      In the CHA algorithm, every virtual call is resolved by only using the hierarchy. Every subclass of the class is considered as target if it contains an implementation of the methods called in the invoke expression.
      Overrides:
      resolveCall in class ClassHierarchyAnalysisAlgorithm
      Parameters:
      method - the method object that contains the given invoke expression in the body.
      invokableStmt - it contains the call which is resolved.
      Returns:
      a stream containing all reachable method signatures after applying the CHA call graph algorithm
